meaning: Regardless of ..., irrespective of ..., whether ... or not. Indicates that the conditions listed in the first part (usually opposites or several possibilities) do not affect the result in the second part.
connection: Noun + にかかわらず; verb dictionary form + verb nai-form + にかかわらず (行く行かないにかかわらず); affirmative and negative (or opposite) forms side by side + にかかわらず (好き嫌いにかかわらず)
usage: The first part is usually a word covering opposites or multiple cases: 天候, 年齢, 性別, 経験の有無, 結果, 好き嫌い, 晴雨, 大小, etc., meaning "in any of these cases ...".
It is also common with affirmative and negative side by side, as in "〜か〜ないかにかかわらず" or "〜〜ないにかかわらず": 参加するしないにかかわらず.
It can be written with kanji as 「に関わらず」, 「に拘わらず」, or 「に拘らず」 with the same meaning; written and official documents more often use hiragana or 「関わらず」.
The second part is usually a neutral statement of the speaker's decision, a rule, or a fact, with no sense of dissatisfaction or surprise — this is the biggest difference from 「にもかかわらず」.
A more colloquial near-synonym is 「〜に関係なく」; a more written one is 「〜を問わず」. To modify a noun, 「〜にかかわりなく」 or 「〜にかかわらない + noun」 (rare) can be used.
scenarios: Stating that there are no restrictions in announcements, job ads, or regulations: 「経験の有無にかかわらず、どなたでも応募できます。」
Event notices saying whether it will be held: 「雨天にかかわらず、イベントは実施します。」
Stating equal pricing or service in business: 「購入金額にかかわらず、送料は無料です。」
Stating general facts in argumentative writing: 「年齢にかかわらず、運動は健康に良い。」
etymology: Formed from 「かかわら」, the irrealis form of the verb 「かかわる」 (関わる／係わる／拘わる, "to be involved in, to concern, to be bound by"), plus the continuative form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. Literally "not being involved with ..., not being bound by ...", it became grammaticalized as "regardless of ...". Since 「ず」 is a classical negative, the pattern has a written, formal feel. In modern Japanese both spellings 「拘わらず」 and 「関わらず」 exist side by side; the standard spelling in the Joyo kanji list is 「関わる」.
examples: Anyone can take part, regardless of age.
The match will go ahead as planned, whatever the weather.
Whether or not you have experience, motivated people are welcome.
Please reply whether or not you will attend.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: With an extra 「も」, the meaning is completely different: it expresses contrast, "despite ..., still ...", where the result goes against expectations, with a tone of surprise or dissatisfaction. 「雨にかかわらず行く」 = I'll go whether it rains or not (the condition doesn't matter); 「雨にもかかわらず行った」 = I went despite the rain (contrast with a fact).

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning as にかかわらず (regardless of), but more written and common in job ads: 「年齢・性別を問わず」. It usually follows pairs of opposite nouns like 男女, 昼夜, 国内外, and generally not affirmative-negative verb pairs.

similar.title: 〜に関係なく
similar.explanation: Same meaning but more colloquial and direct: 「天気に関係なく行きます」. In everyday conversation it is more common than にかかわらず.

meaning: Despite ..., in spite of ..., although .... Expresses contrast: given that the first part is a fact, a result contrary to normal expectations occurs, often with the speaker's surprise, astonishment, dissatisfaction, or reproach.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem (+ である) + にもかかわらず; plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + にもかかわらず; at the start of a sentence 「それにもかかわらず」 (= それなのに)
usage: The first part is an established fact (not a hypothesis), and the second is a contrary, unexpected result: 熱があるにもかかわらず出社した.
Nouns and na-adjectives can attach directly or with 「である」: 雨にもかかわらず／雨であるにもかかわらず; 静かであるにもかかわらず.
It can stand alone at the start of a sentence as a conjunction, 「それにもかかわらず」 or 「にもかかわらず、」, following on from the previous sentence.
The second part is generally a statement of fact and cannot be a command, request, or intention (×雨にもかかわらず来てください is not said).
It can be written 「にも関わらず」 or 「にも拘わらず」; the tone is written and formal, more objective and stiffer than 「のに」.
scenarios: Reporting unusual facts in news and reports: 「多くの反対にもかかわらず、法案は可決された。」
Praising someone for going to the trouble: 「お忙しいにもかかわらず、お越しいただきありがとうございます。」
Criticizing or reproaching: 「何度も注意したにもかかわらず、彼は同じミスを繰り返した。」
Contrast in papers and argumentative writing: 「努力したにもかかわらず、成果は得られなかった。」
etymology: The structure is case particle 「に」 + particle 「も」 + 「かかわらず」. 「かかわらず」 comes from the irrealis form of the verb 「かかわる」 (関わる／拘わる) plus the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」, meaning "not being constrained by ...". With 「も」 added, it literally means "even in such a situation, not being affected by it", which developed into the contrastive "despite ..., still ...". It shares its origin with 「にかかわらず」, but because of the emphatic 「も」, the meaning shifted from "the condition doesn't matter" to "contrast with an actual fact".
examples: Despite the rain, a large crowd gathered.
He came to the office even though he had a fever.
Despite working extremely hard, I didn't pass.
Thank you very much for attending despite your busy schedule.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Also contrastive, but のに is very colloquial and more emotional (dissatisfaction, regret), and the second part can be left unsaid at the end of a sentence: 「せっかく作ったのに…」. にもかかわらず is more written and objective, and the second part must be stated.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: Without 「も」 it means "regardless of ...": the first part is a range of possible conditions unrelated to the result. With にもかかわらず, the first part is a single established fact and the second part contradicts it.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Also expresses contrast, "although ..., ...", but ものの focuses on "the first part is true, but things didn't develop as expected", often about one's own actions (買ったものの使わない); it is weaker than にもかかわらず, with less surprise or reproach.

meaning: There's no way ..., can't possibly ..., it makes no sense that .... The speaker strongly denies, based on reasoning or common sense, that something could happen or be true.
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + わけがない; na-adjective stem + な／である + わけがない; noun + の／である + わけがない
usage: Expresses a strong subjective denial, far more assertive than 「〜ないだろう」: あの人が犯人のわけがない.
「が」 can be replaced with 「は」 (わけはない), and in speech the particle is often dropped: 「できるわけない」.
The polite form is 「わけがありません」; rough colloquial forms are 「わけねえ／わけねーだろ」.
Written 「訳がない」 in kanji, though hiragana is more common in books.
Distinguish it from 「わけではない」 (it's not that ..., partial negation) and 「わけにはいかない」 (can't, for moral reasons); the 「訳ない」 in 「申し訳ない」 is an idiom unrelated to this grammar point.
scenarios: Strongly rejecting someone's guess in everyday conversation: 「そんなこと、私が知るわけがないでしょう。」
Expressing confidence or defiance: 「あんなに練習したんだから、負けるわけがない。」
Refuting an unreasonable claim: 「こんな安い値段で本物のわけがない。」
Often appears in novels and manga dialogue as 「〜わけないだろ！」
etymology: 「わけ」 is written 「訳」 and originally meant "logic, reason, cause of things" (cognate with the verb 「分ける」, "the logic one has discerned"). 「わけがない」 literally means "there's no (such) reason", and by extension "by all logic it's impossible". The kanji 「訳」 was borrowed later to write the word; its meaning "translate" has nothing to do with this.
examples: There's no way a child could solve such a difficult problem.
Someone as serious as him would never lie.
We practiced so much, there's no way we'll lose.
At such a low price, there's no way it's the real thing.

similar.title: 〜はずがない
similar.explanation: Also means "impossible", and the two are mostly interchangeable. はずがない leans toward inference based on specific grounds or plans (I definitely locked it, so it can't have been stolen); わけがない leans toward impossibility by common sense and reasoning, and sounds more subjective and stronger.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: The affirmative わけだ means "no wonder, naturally ...", a conclusion drawn from facts; わけがない denies a possibility. They point in opposite directions.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Expresses partial negation, "it's not that ...": 「嫌いなわけではない」 = it's not that I dislike it. わけがない completely denies a possibility; don't confuse them.

similar.title: 〜わけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Means "can't do" because of social norms or moral obligation, as in 「休むわけにはいかない」; it has nothing to do with judging possibility.

meaning: Have no choice but to ..., can't help but ..., be forced to .... Expresses that because of some situation or pressure one can only do something, even unwillingly; it can also mean "one can't help admitting / saying" from the facts.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ざるを得ない; する → せざるを得ない; 来る → こざるを得ない
usage: Note the special form of する: not ×しざるを得ない but 「せざるを得ない」 (中止せざるを得ない).
Conjugation: ざるを得なかった (past), ざるを得ません (polite); classical form 「ざるを得ず」.
「得ない」 is read 「えない」, and it is also often written in hiragana as 「ざるをえない」.
The subject is usually the speaker, or a third person in an objective description; it carries a sense of resignation: "I didn't want to, but there was no other choice".
With verbs of cognition it means "have to admit": 「彼の才能は認めざるを得ない」.
scenarios: Explaining an unavoidable decision: 「台風のため、イベントは中止せざるを得なかった。」
Reluctantly complying at work: 「上司の命令だから、従わざるを得ない。」
Objective judgments in commentary and reports: 「この結果を見る限り、計画は失敗だったと言わざるを得ない。」
Usable in both writing and formal speech; it conveys more of a sense of being forced than 「しなければならない」.
etymology: 「ざる」 is the attributive form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 (the supplementary conjugation of ず — ざら・ざり・ざる・ざれ — came from the fusion of 「ず＋あり」). 「〜ざる」 can act as a noun-like element, followed by the object marker 「を」 and 「得ない」, the negative of 「得る（える）」, the modern form of the verb 「得（う）」 (to be able, to obtain). Literally "cannot manage not to do ..." — a double negative expressing necessity, and a remnant of classical grammar in modern written Japanese.
examples: It's an order from my boss, so I have no choice but to obey.
A typhoon was approaching, so the match had to be canceled.
With this much evidence, I have to admit it.
Unfortunately, I have to say the plan was a failure.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Expresses obligation or necessity, "must ...", a neutral rule or duty; ざるを得ない stresses "there's no other option, I have to do it against my will", with a sense of resignation and compulsion.

similar.title: 〜ないわけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Also means "can't not do", but the reasons are usually social norms, personal relationships, or morals (you can't not go to a friend's wedding); ざるを得ない is more about being forced by objective circumstances.

similar.title: 〜しかない／〜ほかない
similar.explanation: "Can only ...", meaning there's no other way; more colloquial and calmer in tone. ざるを得ない is more written, with a stronger sense of being forced.

meaning: Nothing more than ..., merely ..., only .... Indicates that a degree, quantity, or status is not high, emphasizing "that's all it is, nothing special".
connection: Noun + にすぎない; plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + にすぎない; na-adjective stem / noun + である + にすぎない
usage: It can also be written with a kanji for すぎ (the one meaning "pass"); both spellings are common in books.
Conjugation: にすぎなかった (past), にすぎません (polite); the classical forms 「にすぎず」 and 「にすぎぬ」 are used to suspend a clause or modify a noun.
Often combined with 「ただ」, 「単なる」, 「ほんの」, or 「〜だけ」 for emphasis: 「単なる噂にすぎない」.
After quantities it stresses a small amount: 「参加者はわずか10人にすぎなかった」.
It carries the speaker's dismissive or modest tone; about oneself it sounds humble: 「私は一社員にすぎません」.
scenarios: Downplaying the value of a claim in essays or commentary: 「それは言い訳にすぎない。」
News reports stressing a small number: 「投票率は30%にすぎなかった。」
Being modest about oneself: 「私は彼の意見を伝えたにすぎません。」
Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation 「〜だけだ」 is more usual.
etymology: Made of the case particle 「に」 + the negative of the verb すぎる (in Classical Japanese the kami-nidan verb すぐ). すぎる originally means "to exceed, to pass", so 「〜にすぎない」 literally means "does not go beyond ... (this degree)", and by extension "is merely ...". In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese, 「〜ニスギズ」 was used to render the Chinese expression for "nothing but ...", and the modern written 「にすぎず」 is a remnant of this form.
examples: That's nothing more than an excuse.
I'm just an ordinary employee, so I don't have the authority to decide.
That story turned out to be nothing more than a rumor.
There were only ten participants, and the venue was almost empty.

similar.title: 〜だけだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning (only ...), but だけだ is a neutral limitation common in speech; にすぎない carries an evaluation of "not worth mentioning, low in degree" and is more written.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: "Is precisely ..., is nothing other than ...", an emphatic assertion (成功は努力の結果にほかならない) with no belittling sense; にすぎない evaluates something as low.

similar.title: 〜でしかない
similar.explanation: "Is only ...", very close to にすぎない and also negative in evaluation; slightly more colloquial.

meaning: Could well ..., might end up ..., there's a risk that .... Expresses the possibility or danger of a bad outcome, with the speaker's concern or warning.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + かねない (なり + かねない → なりかねない; し + かねない → しかねない)
usage: Used only for negative, undesirable outcomes: 事故になりかねない, 誤解を招きかねない. It can't be used for good outcomes (×成功しかねない).
Conjugation: かねなかった (past); the polite form is 「かねません」 — note that it still means "might ..."; don't confuse it with 「かねます」 (can't ...).
Formally it is the negative of 「かねる」, but its meaning isn't simply "can do"; it means "(something bad) could happen".
Often combined with conditions such as 「このままでは」, 「下手をすると」, or 「〜と」: 「このままでは倒産しかねない」.
It can also be used to say someone "is capable of doing such a thing": 「あの人ならやりかねない」.
scenarios: Reminding or warning of a risk: 「スピードを出しすぎると、事故を起こしかねない。」
Predicting negative consequences in news and commentary: 「この政策は経済に悪影響を与えかねない。」
Tactfully pointing out a problem at work: 「その言い方は誤解を招きかねませんよ。」
Commenting on someone's character: 「彼なら約束を忘れかねない。」
etymology: 「かねる」 is written 「兼ねる」, originally meaning "to serve two roles at once, to combine" (大は小を兼ねる, "the large can serve for the small"). It is generally thought that "it's hard to handle two things at once" led to its use as an auxiliary verb after other verbs meaning "find it hard to ..., cannot ..." (→かねる). 「かねない」 is its negative, literally "it's not that it can't", i.e. "it's entirely possible", which then specialized into "something bad may happen". This negative use is thought to have spread from around the early modern period.
examples: At this rate, it could turn into a major accident.
Putting it that way could cause the other person to misunderstand.
He's the type who might say something that cruel.
If it's left alone, it could develop into a big problem.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: The affirmative かねる means "find it hard to ..., cannot ..." (お答えしかねます). かねない means "might ...", almost the opposite; take special care to distinguish 「かねます」 from 「かねません」.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: A neutral "maybe, possibly", usable for good or bad things; かねない is only for bad outcomes, carries a tone of concern or warning, and is more written.

similar.title: 〜おそれがある
similar.explanation: "There's a danger of ..."; very close to かねない, but more objective and written, common in weather forecasts and news (津波のおそれがある). It attaches as verb dictionary form / noun + の + おそれがある.

meaning: Find it difficult to ..., cannot ..., be unable to .... Expresses that, because of psychological reluctance, one's position, or circumstances, one cannot do something even if one wanted to; often used as a polite, indirect refusal.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + かねる (答え + かねる → 答えかねる; いたし + かねます → いたしかねます)
usage: Conjugates as an ichidan verb: かねます, かねました, かねた, かねて. Note that the negative 「かねない」 means something completely different (might ...).
A set polite refusal in service and business settings: 「〜いたしかねます」, 「〜しかねます」, 「〜応じかねます」; softer than 「できません」.
Also used for psychological difficulty in accepting something: 「彼の意見には賛成しかねる」, 「理解しかねる」.
Idiomatic expressions: 「見るに見かねて」 (unable to stand by and watch any longer, ...), 「待ちかねる」 (to grow impatient waiting, to be unable to wait).
It is not used for lack of ability (×泳ぎかねる to mean "can't swim" is wrong); for inability use 「〜できない」.
scenarios: Shop staff or customer service declining a customer's request: 「申し訳ございませんが、返品はお受けいたしかねます。」
Politely declining in business emails: 「ご要望には応じかねますので、ご了承ください。」
Expressing disagreement in a meeting: 「その案には賛成しかねます。」
In narration, being unable to hold back: 「見るに見かねて、手を貸した。」
etymology: 「かねる」 is written 「兼ねる」, originally meaning "to combine, to have both, to serve in two roles at once" (大は小を兼ねる). It is generally thought that "it's hard to handle two things at once" led to its use as an auxiliary verb after the verb continuative form meaning "find it hard to ..."; this use, as 「〜かぬ」 (the classical shimo-nidan 「かぬ」), is already found in Middle Japanese. As an auxiliary verb today it is usually written in hiragana as 「かねる」.
examples: We sincerely apologize, but we are unable to answer questions on that matter.
We regret that we are unable to accommodate your request and ask for your understanding.
I really can't understand his attitude.
I couldn't just stand by and watch, so I helped him out.

similar.title: 〜かねない
similar.explanation: The negative かねない means "could well (lead to something bad)". 「お答えしかねます」 = we cannot answer; 「誤解を招きかねません」 = it may cause a misunderstanding.

similar.title: 〜にくい
similar.explanation: "Hard to ...", usually about physical or objective difficulty (読みにくい字); かねる focuses on psychological difficulty or one's position, and is often a polite refusal.

similar.title: 〜できない
similar.explanation: States directly that one cannot or may not; かねる is an indirect refusal and more appropriate in service and business settings.

meaning: In, at, on ... (a place, time, field, or aspect). Indicates the place, time, or occasion where an action or event takes place, or the scope or field concerned; a written equivalent of 「で」 or 「に」.
connection: Noun + において／においては／においても; to modify a noun: noun + における + noun (noun + においての + noun is also possible)
usage: For places and times it corresponds to 「で」: 「式は講堂において行われる」 = 講堂で行われる, but more formal.
For fields or aspects: 「医学の分野において」, 「この点において」.
To modify a noun use 「における」: 「日本における少子化」, 「現代社会における問題」.
Often combined with 「は」 or 「も」: 「においては」 (contrastive emphasis), 「においても」 (in ... as well).
It can be written 「に於いて」 or 「に於ける」, but modern texts mostly use hiragana. Distinguish it from the verb use 「〜に置いて」 (placing something at ...).
scenarios: Notices for ceremonies and meetings: 「入学式は体育館において挙行いたします。」
Limiting the field in papers and reports: 「経済の分野において、大きな変化が見られる。」
News reports: 「東京における人口集中が問題になっている。」
Rarely used in conversation; everyday speech generally uses 「で」.
etymology: It comes from the case particle 「に」 + 「おい」, the sound-changed continuative form of the verb 「置く（おく）」 (to place), + the conjunctive particle 「て」, literally "placed at ...". In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese, this form was used to render the Chinese preposition 「於」, so it was written 「に於いて」 and gradually became fixed as a written particle for place, time, and scope. 「における」 is generally thought to come from 「おけ」, the realis form of 「置く」, plus 「る」, the attributive form of the classical perfective/continuative auxiliary 「り」, literally "which is placed at ...", used to modify nouns.
examples: The meeting will be held in Conference Room 1.
In modern society, information is extremely important.
I researched the problem of the declining birthrate in Japan.
He also excels in terms of research.

similar.title: 〜で (case particle)
similar.explanation: The most basic way to mark the place or time of an action, used in both speech and writing; において is more formal and written, and can also express abstract fields or scope.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: Means "about ...", marking the topic of talk or thought; において marks the place or field where something occurs, not a topic. 「日本における問題」 (problems that exist in Japan) ≠ 「日本についての問題」 (questions about Japan).

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: "For ..., to ...", marking the standpoint of an evaluation; において marks an occasion or field and cannot express whose standpoint is taken.

meaning: Although ..., (but) .... Acknowledges the first part as fact, but the second part did not develop as the first part would lead one to expect; expresses contrast.
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + ものの; na-adjective stem + な／である + ものの; noun + である + ものの; set forms 「とはいうものの」, 「とはいえ」
usage: The first part is an established fact, and the second is usually a contrary, less-than-ideal situation: 「買ったものの、一度も使っていない」.
Often appears as 「〜たものの」, describing "I did ..., but nothing came of it".
「とはいうものの」 can stand alone at the start of a sentence, meaning "that said, even so": 「とはいうものの、簡単ではない」.
The second part cannot be an intention, command, or request; the tone is fairly written and stresses the gap between the two parts more than 「けれども」 or 「が」.
Nouns cannot take 「ものの」 directly; say 「学生であるものの」.
scenarios: Describing your own experiences that fell short of expectations: 「大学は卒業したものの、まだ仕事が見つからない。」
Describing conflicting feelings in essays: 「頭では分かっているものの、なかなか実行できない。」
Acknowledging something first, then adding a qualification, in reports: 「景気は回復傾向にあるものの、消費はまだ弱い。」
Used in written language and fairly formal speech.
etymology: Made of the formal noun 「もの」 plus the particle 「の」. In Middle Japanese (Heian period) prose, 「ものの」 was already used as a conjunctive particle expressing contrast ("although ..., still"), frequently seen in waka poetry and tales. Modern Japanese inherited this use, which is why it has a somewhat written, literary feel.
examples: I bought a new camera, but I haven't used it even once.
I understand it in my head, but I just can't put it into practice.
I graduated from university, but I still haven't found a job.
Although it's officially spring, the cold days continue.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Also expresses contrast, but のに carries strong dissatisfaction, surprise, or regret and is very colloquial; ものの is calmer, more objective, and written.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: "Despite ..., still", stressing the contrast and surprise, mostly about others or objective facts; ものの is mostly used for the speaker's own "I did it, but nothing came of it".

similar.title: 〜けれども／〜が
similar.explanation: General contrast or lead-in, the most widely used; ものの only expresses a turn where the facts of the first part don't match the expected outcome.

meaning: 1) While ...ing (two actions at the same time, written); 2) 「〜つつも」: although ..., (still) ... (contrast); 3) 「〜つつある」: be in the process of ..., gradually ... (an ongoing change).
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + つつ／つつも／つつある
usage: For simultaneity it is the same as 「ながら」 but more written: 「景色を楽しみつつ歩く」. Both actions must have the same subject.
「つつも」 expresses contrast and often combines with verbs like 「知る」, 「思う」, 「言う」, 「分かる」: 「悪いと知りつつも嘘をついた」.
「つつある」 expresses a state changing in a certain direction, mostly with verbs of change: 「回復しつつある」, 「減りつつある」. It is not used for actions that end instantly.
「つつ」 itself doesn't conjugate; 「つつある」 conjugates like ある: つつあった, つつあります.
Common in written language, news, and papers; in speech people generally say 「ながら」 or 「ている」.
scenarios: News reports describing trends: 「景気は少しずつ回復しつつある。」
Describing inner conflict in essays and novels: 「体に悪いと思いつつも、タバコがやめられない。」
Letters and speeches: 「皆様のご健康をお祈りしつつ、筆を置きます。」
Replacing ながら in formal writing, e.g. deciding on one's future path 「両親と相談しつつ」 (while consulting one's parents).
etymology: 「つつ」 is a Classical Japanese conjunctive particle already used extensively in Old Japanese texts such as the Man'yōshū, expressing repetition or continuation of an action, or two actions at once. One theory derives it from the reduplication of the perfective auxiliary 「つ」. In waka poetry it often ended a poem to leave a lingering effect (the 「〜つつ」 ending, as in "わが衣手は露にぬれつつ"). The contrastive meaning of 「つつも」 and the progressive meaning of 「つつある」 both developed from the basic sense of "continuing, simultaneous".
examples: I knew it was wrong, but I lied anyway.
The economy is gradually recovering.
I know it's bad for my health, but I can't quit smoking.
I walked along the mountain path while gazing at the beautiful scenery.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: The most common way to say "while ...ing", used in both speech and writing; つつ is more written and literary. For contrast, 「ながら（も）」 can follow nouns and adjectives (狭いながらも), while 「つつも」 only follows verbs.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Expresses an ongoing action or continuing state; 「つつある」 stresses "in the process of changing in a direction, not yet complete", is more written, and is only used with verbs of change.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Also contrastive, but with ものの the first part is a completed fact; 「つつも」 mostly expresses acting contrary to what one knows or thinks.

meaning: 1) After ... (and then), on the basis of ...: first complete the first action, then do the second on that basis (〜た上で／noun の上で); 2) in ..., in the process of ..., in terms of ... (〜る上で／〜上では): when doing something, or from a certain perspective.
connection: 1) Verb ta-form + 上で; noun + の + 上で (相談の上で, 確認の上で); 2) verb dictionary form + 上で(では／も); noun + の + 上で(は) (仕事の上で)
usage: 「た上で」 stresses first doing the first action properly and then, carefully, doing the second on the basis of its result: 「よく考えた上で決めてください」. The second part is usually an important decision or action.
「Dictionary form + 上で」 means "when ..., in order to ...": 「〜を学ぶ上で大切なこと」 (what matters when learning ...); the second part is usually an evaluation such as "important, necessary, care, problem".
「Noun の上では」 means "from the standpoint of ..., in terms of ...": 「計算の上では可能だ」, 「法律の上では問題ない」.
To modify a noun use 「上での」: 「話し合った上での結論」.
Don't confuse it with the physical location 「机の上で」 (on the desk); it is also often written in hiragana as 「うえで」.
scenarios: Explaining business procedures: 「内容を確認した上で、署名してください。」
Serious decisions: 「家族と相談の上で、転職を決めました。」
Study tips and lessons learned, e.g. saying that when learning a foreign language (〜を学ぶ上で), 「一番大切なのは継続だ。」
Qualifying a statement in argumentative writing: 「データの上では、売り上げは伸びている。」
etymology: Made of the noun 「上（うえ）」 plus the case particle 「で」. 「上」 originally means "above, on top" in space, and extended to "on top of something = on its basis, after it" and "in terms of ..., in matters of ...". This extension from spatial to abstract meanings (order, field) is seen in Japanese from the Middle Japanese period onward (e.g. 「身の上」, "one's circumstances"). (Compare English "on top of that" and "upon reflection".)
examples: Please make your decision after thinking it over carefully.
What's the most important thing in learning a foreign language?
After discussing it with my parents, I decided to study abroad.
Please sign after checking the contents.

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: Simply expresses time order; た上で stresses that the second action is done "on the basis of the first, after the first has been done thoroughly", implying care.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: Expresses order, "after ...", common in speech; た上で is more written and stresses that the first action is a necessary prerequisite for the second.

similar.title: 〜において
similar.explanation: Expresses a field or occasion, "in ..."; when 「〜上で」 expresses a field it usually pairs with evaluations like "important, necessary, problem", and it can follow the verb dictionary form (生きていく上で).

meaning: 1) As long as ... (then ...): the second part holds while the state in the first part continues (〜限り); 2) unless ...: 〜ない限り; 3) as far as ..., to the extent of ...: 〜限りでは (知る限りでは); 4) as ... as possible: できる限り, 力の限り; 5) limited to ... only: 〜に限り (本日に限り).
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている form / nai-form + 限り; noun + である + 限り; verb ta-form / ている form + 限りでは; noun + の + 限り; noun + に + 限り
usage: 「〜限り」 marks the boundary of a condition: 「生きている限り」 = as long as I'm alive. The second part is usually the speaker's resolution or judgment.
「〜ない限り」 = "unless ..., (not) ...", expressing the sole condition: 「謝らない限り、許さない」.
「〜限りでは」 follows verbs of cognition (知る, 聞く, 見る, 調べる) to limit the scope of information: 「私の知る限りでは」.
「できる限り」 and 「力の限り」 express the maximum extent; 「〜に限り」 means "limited to", common in ads and notices.
Both the kanji 「限り」 and hiragana 「かぎり」 are common. Note that 「限りない」 (limitless) is an adjective, different from this grammar point.
scenarios: Expressing determination: 「体が動く限り、仕事を続けたい。」
Setting a condition: 「よほどのことがない限り、会議は予定通り行います。」
Stating information cautiously: 「私が調べた限りでは、問題は見つかりませんでした。」
Shop notices: 「本日に限り、全品半額です。」
etymology: 「限り」 is the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「限る（かぎる）」, originally meaning "boundary, limit, end". Theories differ about the earlier origin of 「限る」, but its core meaning has always been "to set a boundary, to limit". From "boundary" it extended to "within the range of (as long as)", "reaching the limit (doing one's utmost)", and "restricting (only)". Classical Japanese also had 「〜の限り」 meaning "all, every" (e.g. "あるかぎり").
examples: As far as I know, he's someone you can trust.
As long as it doesn't rain, the match will be held.
As long as my stamina holds out, I want to keep running.
Today only, everything is half price.
As far as I could tell from my research, there were no problems.

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Uses the same verb 「限る」 but means "not necessarily ...", a partial negation; completely different from 「限り」 (as long as, limited to).

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: "While ...", stressing doing something before the state changes; 限り means "as long as that state continues, the second part holds", stressing the condition rather than the timing.

similar.title: 〜さえ〜ば
similar.explanation: "As long as ...", stressing the sole condition (お金さえあれば); 「〜限り」 focuses more on "for the period this state continues" and carries a tone of determination or assertion.

meaning: Tend to ..., apt to ..., often .... Expresses that some (usually undesirable) state or tendency often appears, even if unintentionally.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + がち; noun + がち (病気がち, 留守がち, 遠慮がち); conjugates like a na-adjective: がちだ／がちな + noun／がちの + noun／がちで／がちになる
usage: Mostly used for negative tendencies: 忘れがち, 遅れがち, 怠けがち, 病気がち. It sounds unnatural with good things (×成功しがち).
The set combinations with nouns are limited: 病気がち, 留守がち, 曇りがち, 遠慮がち, 伏し目がち, etc.
To modify a noun use 「がちな」 or 「がちの」: 「ありがちな話」, 「曇りがちの天気」.
「ありがち」 (common, clichéd) has become an everyday word in its own right.
It refers to a natural tendency or high frequency, not inevitability; often combined with 「つい」, 「どうしても」, or 「〜と」.
scenarios: Describing health or lifestyle habits: 「冬は風邪をひきがちだ。」
Weather forecasts: 「明日は曇りがちの天気となるでしょう。」
Reflecting on yourself or reminding others: 「忙しいと、つい食事を抜きがちになる。」
Commenting on common failings: 「若者にありがちな失敗だ。」
etymology: 「がち」 is generally thought to be the voiced form of the noun 「勝ち（かち）」 (winning). 「勝ち」 originally meant "prevailing, having the upper hand", and after other words it meant "a certain element predominates", as in 「黒勝ち」 (mostly black) or 「涙がち」 (often in tears); from this it extended to "... tends to appear, a strong tendency toward ...". The form 「〜がちなり」 is already found in classical texts.
examples: In winter I just tend to catch colds.
Lately the weather has been mostly cloudy.
He was often sick as a child and frequently missed school.
When I'm busy, I tend to skip meals.

similar.title: 〜やすい
similar.explanation: "Easy to ...", meaning the action itself is easy to do or likely to happen (分かりやすい, 壊れやすい), for good or bad; がち means some undesirable tendency often appears, stressing frequency.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Means "having a feel of ..., prone to ..." (忘れっぽい, 子供っぽい), more colloquial and mostly about personality traits; がち refers more to a temporary tendency and is more written.

similar.title: 〜だらけ
similar.explanation: Means "full of ..., covered in ...", about large quantities spread over a surface; がち expresses tendency or frequency.

meaning: Full of ..., covered in ..., nothing but .... Expresses that there is too much of something (usually bad or unpleasant), spread all over.
connection: Noun + だらけ; conjugates like a na-adjective / noun: だらけだ／だらけの + noun／だらけで／だらけになる
usage: Mostly used for negative things: 泥だらけ, 傷だらけ, 血だらけ, ゴミだらけ, 間違いだらけ, 借金だらけ.
It can refer to a surface physically covered in something (泥だらけの靴) or to being "full of" something abstract (矛盾だらけ, 問題だらけ).
To modify a noun use 「だらけの」: 「傷だらけの手」.
It carries the speaker's dissatisfaction or distaste and is generally not used for positive things (×花だらけ usually sounds odd unless there's a sense of "far too many").
Distinguish it from the verb 「だらける」 (to slack off, be lazy): 「だらけた生活」 is not this grammar point.
scenarios: Describing appearance: 「子供たちは泥だらけになって遊んでいた。」
Criticizing writing or work: 「この報告書は間違いだらけだ。」
Describing surroundings: 「部屋はゴミだらけで、足の踏み場もない。」
Common in both everyday speech and writing.
etymology: 「だらけ」 is a suffix whose origin is debated, with several theories and no consensus. One theory links it to words like 「だらだら」 and 「だらける」, which express things clinging all over or a loose, slack state; another holds that it is a sound change of an old suffix meaning "full of". It is not normally written with kanji. What is certain is that it gradually spread in colloquial speech from the early modern period onward, meaning "all over, full of".
examples: The children were playing and got covered in mud.
This essay is full of mistakes.
The room is full of garbage; there's nowhere to step.
Seeing my grandfather's scarred hands, I thought of all the hardships he'd been through.

similar.title: 〜まみれ
similar.explanation: Also means "covered in", but only for liquids, powders, etc. coating a surface (汗まみれ, 泥まみれ, 血まみれ), and can't be used for abstract quantities like "間違いまみれ"; だらけ has a wider range.

similar.title: 〜ずくめ
similar.explanation: Means "entirely, nothing but" and can be used for good things (いいことずくめ, 黒ずくめの服); だらけ is mostly negative.

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: Expresses a tendency, something that often happens; だらけ expresses a large quantity spread all over.

meaning: 1) Along ... (a river, road, or other long, linear thing); 2) in line with ..., following ... (a policy, plan, expectations, etc.), keeping one's actions consistent with it.
connection: Noun + に沿って／に沿い; to modify a noun: noun + に沿った／に沿う + noun
usage: Concrete meaning: follows nouns for things that extend in a line: 川, 道, 線路, 海岸, 壁, etc.: 「川に沿って歩く」.
Abstract meaning: follows nouns for policies, expectations, or standards: 方針, 計画, マニュアル, 希望, 要望, 趣旨: 「方針に沿って」.
The written suspended form is 「に沿い」; to modify a noun use 「に沿った」 or 「に沿う」: 「ご要望に沿ったプラン」.
In 「ご期待に沿えるよう努力します」 (we will do our best to live up to your expectations), 「沿える」 is the potential form; this phrase is also very common.
The kanji 「沿う」 and 「添う」 are read the same; for "follow, conform to", modern texts mostly write 「沿う」, and the hiragana 「にそって」 is also seen.
scenarios: Describing scenery or routes: 「川に沿って桜並木が続いている。」
Work instructions, e.g. carrying out tasks 「マニュアルにそって」 (according to the manual).
Business proposals: 「お客様のご要望に沿ったプランをご提案します。」
Formal statements: 「ご期待に沿えるよう、全力を尽くします。」
etymology: From the verb 「沿う（そう）」, originally meaning "to go along something, to move close beside it". It is generally thought to share its origin with 「添う（そう）」, meaning "to accompany, to be added to". From physically "following along a long object" it extended to the abstract "acting in line with a policy or expectations, staying consistent with them". 「沿って」 is the te-form of 「沿う」 (with a geminate sound change). (Compare English "along the lines of ...".)
examples: A row of cherry trees runs along the river.
Please carry out the work according to the manual.
We will propose a plan that meets the customer's requests.
In line with company policy, a new system was introduced.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: "Based on ..., on the basis of ...": the first part is the grounds or basis (データ, 法律, 事実), and the second arises from it; に沿って means "following, in line with", keeping actions consistent with a policy or expectations, without stressing "grounds".

similar.title: 〜に従って
similar.explanation: "In accordance with" instructions or rules (指示に従って), with a stronger sense of obedience; it can also mean "as ... (changes)" (年をとるに従って). に沿って focuses more on "not deviating from the direction".

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Expresses means, cause, basis, or "differs depending on ...", with a wide range of uses; に沿って only means "along" or "in line with".

meaning: Based on ..., on the basis of ..., grounded in .... Indicates that a judgment, action, or creation in the second part is based on, grounded in, or starts from the first part.
connection: Noun + に基づいて／に基づき; to modify a noun: noun + に基づく／に基づいた + noun
usage: The first part is usually something that can serve as a basis: データ, 事実, 法律, 規則, 調査結果, 経験, 計画, 実話, etc.
The written suspended form is 「に基づき」; to modify a noun use 「に基づく」 or 「に基づいた」: 「法律に基づく手続き」.
「〜は…に基づいている」 means "... is based on ...": 「この映画は実話に基づいている」.
In modern kana it is spelled 「もとづく」 (with づ, not ず), because it comes from 「もと＋つく」.
Common in written language and formal settings; in speech you can say 「〜をもとに」.
scenarios: Reports and papers: 「調査結果に基づいて、改善案を作成した。」
Legal and administrative documents: 「法律に基づき、適切に処理いたします。」
Introducing a work: 「この映画は実話に基づいている。」
Business decisions: 「データに基づいた判断が求められる。」
etymology: 「基づく」 is made of the noun 「基（もと）」 (root, foundation) plus the verb 「付く（つく）」 (to attach), with 「つく」 voiced to 「づく」. Literally "attached to the foundation", it extended to "to be grounded in ...". Precisely because it comes from 「つく」, modern kana spelling rules require 「もとづく」.
examples: This movie is based on a true story.
It's important to make judgments based on data.
Please follow the procedures prescribed by law.
Based on the survey results, we drew up a new plan.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: Acting "in line with, following" a policy or expectations, stressing not deviating; に基づいて stresses that the first part is the grounds or basis from which the second is derived or built.

similar.title: 〜をもとに（して）
similar.explanation: "Using ... as material or a basis", mostly for creative work or production (小説をもとに映画を作る), more colloquial; に基づいて stresses the legitimacy of the basis and is more written.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: When it means "according to" (規則によって) it is close to に基づいて, but によって also has many other uses: cause, means, the agent in passives, etc.

meaning: Not necessarily ..., not always .... Indicates that something generally taken for granted has exceptions; a partial negation. 「〜ないとも限らない」 means "one can't rule out that ..., ... may well happen".
connection: Plain form (after nouns and na-adjective stems, だ may be added or omitted) + とは限らない; often combined with 「必ずしも」, 「いつも」, 「誰でも」, or 「〜からといって」
usage: Common combinations: 「必ずしも〜とは限らない」, 「〜からといって〜とは限らない」, 「いつも〜とは限らない」.
Polite: とは限りません; written suspended form: とは限らず.
「〜ないとも限らない」 is a double negative meaning a certain (usually bad) possibility exists: 「事故が起きないとも限らない」.
Used to counter stereotypes or point out exceptions; it signals "there are exceptions" more clearly than 「〜わけではない」.
The verb is the negative of 「限る」; both the kanji 「限らない」 and hiragana 「かぎらない」 are common.
scenarios: Arguing a point: 「高い物が必ずしも良いとは限らない。」
Correcting a stereotype: 「日本人だからといって、皆が寿司を好きだとは限りません。」
Reminders and advice: 「天気予報が当たるとは限らないから、傘を持っていこう。」
Warning of a possibility: 「誰かに見られないとも限らない。」
etymology: Made of the quotative particle 「と」 + the topic particle 「は」 + 「限らない」, the negative of the verb 「限る」. 「限る」 means "to limit, to be restricted to", so 「〜とは限らない」 literally means "it is not limited to the case of ...", i.e. "there are other cases, not necessarily". 「は」 serves to contrast and limit the scope of the negation, producing a partial negation.
examples: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
Just because someone is Japanese doesn't mean they all like sushi.
The weather forecast isn't always right, so let's take an umbrella.
If you let your guard down, an accident could well happen.

similar.title: 〜限り
similar.explanation: Uses the same verb 「限る」, but 「限り」 means "as long as ..., limited to ..., to the utmost ...", completely different from the partial negation "not necessarily".

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Also a partial negation, "it's not that ...", focusing on denying an inference the listener might draw (嫌いなわけではない); とは限らない focuses on pointing out that "exceptions exist" and often pairs with 「必ずしも」.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Expresses possibility, "maybe"; 「〜ないとも限らない」 also expresses possibility but in a more pessimistic tone, stressing "it can't be ruled out".

meaning: Not only ... but (even) .... Beyond the first item, there is a second of even greater degree; expresses addition, with the second part often marked by 「も」, 「まで」, or 「さえ」.
connection: Noun + ばかりか; plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + ばかりか; na-adjective stem + な／である + ばかりか
usage: The second part often uses 「〜も」, 「〜まで」, or 「〜さえ」: 「漢字ばかりか、ひらがなさえ書けない」.
The second part usually goes a step further than the first (better or worse), with the speaker's surprise or strong feeling.
It can't be used when the second part is a command, request, or intention (e.g. ✕ "Study not only English but Chinese too!" with ばかりか ... 勉強しなさい); use 「だけでなく」 instead.
In speech the form 「ばっかりか」 is also heard.
Note that 「ばかりか」 in 「〜たばかりかもしれない」 is 「ばかり＋かもしれない」, not this grammar point.
scenarios: Describing surprising facts: 「彼は宿題をしないばかりか、授業中に寝ている。」
Recommendations and reviews: 「この店は安いばかりか、味もいい。」
Describing a situation getting worse: 「雨ばかりか、風まで強くなってきた。」
Used in written language and fairly formal speech.
etymology: Made of the adverbial particle 「ばかり」 plus the particle 「か」. 「ばかり」 is generally thought to come from 「はかり」, the continuative form of the verb 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure), originally meaning "about, approximately" (an estimate), later developing the limiting sense "only, just". 「か」 was originally a particle of questions and rhetorical questions, so 「〜ばかりか」 literally means something like "is it only ...?", and from this rhetorical question came the additive meaning "not only ... (but something more)".
examples: Not only does he not do his homework, he even sleeps in class.
This shop is not only cheap, but the food is good too.
Not only is it raining, but the wind has picked up too.
She can speak not only English but French as well.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning, "not only ... but also", but plainer in tone; ばかりか puts more stress on the surprising degree of the second part. Neither is commonly used with commands or requests.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: The most common "not only ... but also", used in speech and writing; the second part can be a command, request, or intention. ばかりか is more written and exclamatory.

similar.title: 〜どころか
similar.explanation: "Far from ..., on the contrary / even ...", often rejecting the first part and presenting an opposite or extreme fact (儲かるどころか損をした); ばかりか accepts the first part and adds to it.
